title: Restricted PBW basis and presentation by basis p-relations
statement: Let $F$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field]. Let $L$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $F$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], equipped with a restricted operation $x\mapsto x^{[p]}$: for $c\in F$ and $x,y\in L$ it satisfies $(cx)^{[p]}=c^px^{[p]}$, $\operatorname{ad}(x^{[p]})=\operatorname{ad}(x)^p$, and $(x+y)^{[p]}=x^{[p]}+y^{[p]}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}s_i(x,y)$. Here $i s_i(x,y)$ is the coefficient of $t^{i-1}$ in $\operatorname{ad}(tx+y)^{p-1}(x)$, computed in $L\otimes_F F[t]$, and $\operatorname{ad}(x)(y)=[x,y]$. Let $T_F(L)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}L^{\otimes_F m}$, with multiplication by concatenation, and write $\iota:L\to T_F(L)$ for its degree-one inclusion. Define $u(L)$ to be the quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by $\iota(x)\iota(y)-\iota(y)\iota(x)-\iota([x,y])$ and $\iota(x)^p-\iota(x^{[p]})$ for all $x,y\in L$. Fix any ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $L$, where $n\ge0$, and write $\bar e_i$ for its images in $u(L)$. Then the monomials $\bar e_1^{a_1}\cdots\bar e_n^{a_n}$, indexed by $0\le a_i<p$, form an $F$-basis of $u(L)$. Moreover its defining ideal in $T_F(L)$ is already generated by $\iota(e_i)\iota(e_j)-\iota(e_j)\iota(e_i)-\iota([e_i,e_j])$ for $1\le i,j\le n$ and $\iota(e_i)^p-\iota(e_i^{[p]})$ for $1\le i\le n$. For $n=0$ the sole basis monomial is $1$.

source.place: Definition 10.39 and Theorem 10.40, printed pp.206--207; the first two sentences of the proof of 10.40 say that the central basis elements c_i generate the kernel, and the rest proves the truncated monomial basis.

proof.text: Put $T=T_F(L)$ and $r(x,y)=\iota(x)\iota(y)-\iota(y)\iota(x)-\iota([x,y])$. If $x=\sum_i a_i e_i$ and $y=\sum_j b_j e_j$, bilinearity gives $r(x,y)=\sum_{i,j}a_i b_j r(e_i,e_j)$. Thus the bracket ideal $R$ is already generated by the basis bracket relations. Set $U=T/R$ and write $j:L\to U$ for its linear map and $E_i=j(e_i)$. Apply [lem-sfb-field-filtered-pbw] over $F$: $E^m=E_1^{m_1}\cdots E_n^{m_n}$ is a basis, and the terms with $|m|=\sum_i m_i\le d$ are a basis of $U_{\le d}$; set $U_{\le-1}=0$. Products of elements of $U_{\le r}$ and $U_{\le s}$ lie in $U_{\le r+s}$ by concatenating words.

source.place: Theorem 10.36 and the tensor-quotient construction, printed p.200; setup for Theorem 10.40.

proof.text: For $x\in L$ put $c(x)=j(x)^p-j(x^{[p]})$. Apply the sum identity of [lem-sfb-associative-jacobson-identities] in $U$. Since $j$ is linear and preserves brackets, it carries each coefficient-defined $s_i(x,y)$ to $s_i(j(x),j(y))$. Subtracting the restricted sum axiom therefore gives $c(x+y)=c(x)+c(y)$. Likewise centrality of the scalars of $F$ and the restricted scalar axiom give $c(ax)=a^p c(x)$. Consequently $c(\sum_i a_i e_i)=\sum_i a_i^p c(e_i)$. Hence the two-sided ideal generated by all $c(x)$ is $I=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$, where $c_i=c(e_i)$, and $u(L)$ is canonically $U/I$. Indeed a map out of either tensor quotient annihilates exactly the bracket relations and all $p$-relations, so the quotient maps in both directions induced by the identity of $T$ are inverse.

source.place: Definition 10.39, printed p.206; first sentence on the kernel in the proof of Theorem 10.40, printed p.207.

proof.text: By the adjoint identity of [lem-sfb-associative-jacobson-identities] and the restricted adjoint axiom, for $x,y\in L$ we have $[c(x),j(y)]=\operatorname{ad}(j(x))^p(j(y))-j([x^{[p]},y])=j(\operatorname{ad}(x)^p(y)-[x^{[p]},y])=0$. This extends from the generators $j(y)$ to all products and linear combinations, using $[c,ab]=[c,a]b+a[c,b]$. Thus each $c_i$ is central in $U$. This uses every restricted axiom but does not assume $x^{[p]}=0$.

source.place: Definition 10.39, printed p.206; centrality assertion in the proof of Theorem 10.40, printed p.207.

proof.text: For $0\le a_i<p$ and $b_i\ge0$ put $B_{a,b}=E^a c_1^{b_1}\cdots c_n^{b_n}$ and $D=|a|+p|b|$. The product expansion using $c_i=E_i^p-j(e_i^{[p]})$ has leading word $E^a E_1^{pb_1}\cdots E_n^{pb_n}$; every other term has word length at most $D-(p-1)\le D-1$, since $j(e_i^{[p]})\in U_{\le1}$ and $p\ge2$. Swapping adjacent generators changes a word of length $D$ by a word of length $D-1$, through $E_i E_j-E_j E_i=j([e_i,e_j])$. Repeating these swaps orders the leading word. Thus $B_{a,b}-E^{a+pb}\in U_{\le D-1}$. By [lem-sfb-field-filtered-pbw] this difference is a linear combination of $E^m$ with $|m|<D$. The correspondence $(a,b)\mapsto a+pb$ is a bijection onto $\mathbf N^n$, by division with remainder in each coordinate.

source.place: Last argument in the proof of Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: comparison with ordinary PBW; expanded leading-word calculation.

proof.text: The triangular formula of step 4 proves that the $B_{a,b}$ form a basis of $U$. For spanning, induct on $|m|$: for $|m|=0$ the monomial is $B_{0,0}=1$; write $m=a+pb$, subtract $B_{a,b}$ from $E^m$, and expand the difference in the lower-degree PBW monomials from [lem-sfb-field-filtered-pbw], to which the induction applies. For independence, take a finite relation among the $B_{a,b}$ and let $D$ be the largest $|a|+p|b|$ with nonzero coefficient. Modulo $U_{\le D-1}$ its degree-$D$ terms are distinct $E^{a+pb}$, which are independent modulo $U_{\le D-1}$ by the filtered-basis clause of [lem-sfb-field-filtered-pbw]. Their coefficients are zero, a contradiction. This finite argument needs no completed algebra.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: why the mixed monomials form a basis; ordinary degree induction and maximal-degree argument.

proof.text: Since the $c_i$ are central, every element of $I$ is a sum $\sum_i v_i c_i$ with $v_i\in U$. Expand $v_i$ in the mixed basis: $B_{a,b}c_i=B_{a,b+\delta_i}$. Therefore $I$ is contained in the span of the $B_{a,b}$ with $b\ne0$. Conversely each such $B_{a,b}$ factors by some $c_i$ with $b_i>0$, so lies in $I$. The complementary mixed basis vectors $B_{a,0}=E^a$ consequently project to a basis of $U/I=u(L)$, giving exactly the claimed truncated monomials. Explicitly their residue classes span, and a linear combination in $I$ must have zero coefficients because the two sets of mixed basis vectors are disjoint.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: quotient by the central basis elements; explicit basis-coordinate argument.

proof.text: Let $K\subset T$ be the ideal generated by $R$ and the $\iota(e_i)^p-\iota(e_i^{[p]})$. In $T/K$ all brackets hold, and the formula $c(\sum_i a_i e_i)=\sum_i a_i^p c_i$ of step 2 shows that every $p$-relation vanishes. Thus $K$ contains the full defining ideal; the reverse inclusion holds because its generators are defining relations. Step 1 replaces $R$ by its basis bracket generators, proving the second clause. When $n=0$, $L=0$, $T=F$ and $0^{[p]}=0$ by the scalar axiom with scalar zero. All relation generators vanish and the empty product $1$ is the only basis vector, in agreement with the preceding arguments.

source.place: Definition 10.39 and Theorem 10.40, printed pp.206--207: tensor-level presentation and empty-basis case.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207, with ordinary PBW Theorem 10.36 and Jacobson Proposition 10.38, printed pp.200--206; the proof expands the central-element, triangular-basis and quotient arguments.
